# The Vanishing Night

On the evening of November 9, 1965, a misconfigured relay at a generating station on the Canadian side of Niagara Falls tripped, and the failure rippled outward through the grid like a stone dropped in still water. Within minutes, thirty million people across Ontario and the northeastern United States were without electricity. In New York City, elevators froze, subways halted, and the skyline—for the first time in decades—went dark. Then something peculiar happened. People walked outside and looked up. Stories spread of callers phoning police stations and newspapers to ask about a vast, glowing cloud hanging over Manhattan. It was the Milky Way, which most of them had never seen from a city, and some had never seen at all. The details are probably embellished; such stories always are. But they survive because they capture something true: most of us now live and die without ever meeting the night face to face.

We tend to think of night as simply the absence of day—a default setting, nothing in itself. But for nearly all of human history, night was a country with its own geography, its own laws, its own customs and dangers and liberties. Until roughly two centuries ago, every human being who ever lived spent half of every existence inside a darkness deeper than anything most of us will ever encounter, broken only by fire, by the moon, and by whatever courage a person could carry into it like a lantern.

Consider the economics of light, because light was once a commodity like bread. A tallow candle—animal fat, rendered and wicked—smoked and stank and guttered, but it was what ordinary households could afford, and even it was rationed like sugar. Beeswax burned clean and bright and cost several times more, which is why it belonged to churches and the rich. The poorest families burned rushlights: dried rushes dipped in kitchen grease, giving off a feeble sputter worth pennies. To read by candlelight for an evening was to burn money. So people arranged their lives around the sun, not from piety but from arithmetic. They went to bed at dusk and rose with it, and the moon did the heavy lifting outdoors. Full-moon nights were working nights; the harvest moon, rising near sunset for several evenings around the equinox, was so useful to farmers gathering crops that it earned its name.

Here is where the old night gets genuinely strange. The historian Roger Ekirch, combing diaries, letters, court records, and medical texts going back centuries, noticed something odd: again and again, writers referred matter-of-factly to "first sleep" and "second sleep," as though sleep arrived in two installments. It did. Before artificial light stretched the evening indefinitely, people went to bed a few hours after dusk, slept deeply for three or four hours, and then woke—not fitfully, but naturally, around midnight, into a calm interval lasting an hour or more. Ekirch called it segmented sleep, and he found it described across centuries and cultures. In the watch, people prayed, read by the light of embers, talked, made love—physicians of the era considered it the best time for conception—smoked, visited neighbors, or simply lay thinking while the house breathed around them. Then they returned to bed and slept until dawn.

This is not merely a curiosity of the archive. In the 1990s, the researcher Thomas Wehr ran an experiment that accidentally recreated the old world: volunteers given fourteen hours of darkness each day, mimicking a winter's natural photoperiod, gradually settled into exactly the pattern Ekirch had documented—a solid block of sleep, a quiet interlude of drowsy wakefulness, another block of sleep. During the interlude, their bodies seeped prolactin, a hormone associated with calm. Subjects described the state as something like meditation, a form of consciousness with no modern name. Which raises an uncomfortable thought: the millions who wake at three in the morning and lie awake, anxious, convinced they are broken—many of them may simply be experiencing an ancient rhythm that our brightly prolonged evenings have disguised, and that our panic about it converts into insomnia. We invented the eight-hour block, then pathologized everyone whose body remembers otherwise.

Night was also, for all its dangers, a kind of commons. The word *curfew* descends from *couvre-feu*—"cover the fire"—the bell that ordered hearths banked and citizens indoors, and behind the bell walked the watchmen with their lanterns and staffs. Cities feared the dark: footpads, cutthroats, ghosts, the devil himself, whom folklore stationed abroad between midnight and cockcrow. But the same darkness that threatened the respectable sheltered everyone else. The enslaved fled north following the Drinking Gourd, the dipper of stars that wheels around the pole. Lovers slipped out. Poachers moved through the squire's woods. The poor, the outlawed, the restless—night was their territory, the one jurisdiction where the powerful were as blind as anyone else. Darkness confiscated wealth. For a few hours, the world reverted to something like equality, governed by whoever knew it best.

It was also a world heard more than seen. Deprived of sight, the preindustrial mind navigated by ear and nose: the creak of a signboard, a dog's bark changing direction, rain arriving over the hills, the smell of a neighbor's chimney smoke meaning someone was awake. And because the eye supplied so little, imagination supplied the rest. The dark was populated—by the mare, the demon of Old English *nightmare*, who sat on sleepers' chests and rode them through bad dreams; by revenants and will-o'-the-wisps; by every anxiety given a body. Folklore looks quaint now, but it functioned as technology: a set of rules and stories for managing fear in an environment where fear was reasonable. We replaced it with floodlights, which manage fear by abolishing the environment altogether.

Above all of this hung the stars. Under a sky unpolluted by artificial light, several thousand stars are visible on a clear moonless night, and the Milky Way is not a rumor but a fact of architecture—a river, a road, a tree, depending on the culture doing the naming. The Aboriginal astronomers of Australia read the dark lanes within it and saw the Emu in the Sky, a constellation made not of stars but of darkness itself, which tells you something about how closely they looked. Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific holding star paths in memory. Fugitives steered by the North Star. And every gaze upward was a gaze backward in time: the light of Andromeda, visible to the naked eye from dark places, left that galaxy two and a half million years ago, before any human existed to see it. The night sky was the oldest library, open every clear night, free to anyone who looked up.

The conquest of this world began, as conquests do, with commerce. Whalers hunted sperm whales for the spermaceti in their heads, which burned brighter and cleaner than tallow, and by the eighteenth century the oceans were being emptied to light drawing rooms. Then came gas. In 1807, an entrepreneur named Frederick Winsor illuminated London's Pall Mall with coal gas to celebrate a royal birthday, and within a generation gasworks were humming at the edges of great cities, lamplighters were a profession with its own ladders and poles, and Paris—glowing—was earning the name City of Light. Travelers wrote of seeing the dome of brightness over a metropolis from miles away, a new kind of landmark: civilization announcing itself to the darkness, and beginning to push it back.

Then, in 1879, Thomas Edison's team produced a practical incandescent bulb, and in 1882 his Pearl Street station began sending electricity to a few dozen customers in lower Manhattan. The acceleration afterward is familiar: arc lights, the white ways of Broadway, electric advertising shouting all night, factories discovering they could run around the clock, and finally the screen—a private sun we carry into bed. Within three generations, a rhythm that had governed every organism on Earth for four billion years became optional for one species. We did not merely illuminate the night. We redefined it: no longer a country with its own laws, but underused daytime, an inefficiency to be corrected.

The night, it turns out, was not empty. It was habitat. Consider the sea turtle, which has managed its affairs for a hundred million years using one simple rule: crawl toward the brighter horizon, which, on a natural beach, is the ocean reflecting the sky. A beachfront lined with hotels reverses the rule. Hatchlings pour from the sand and march inland, toward the glow, into roads and pools and exhaustion; entire coastal towns now pass lighting ordinances during nesting season, dimming themselves for creatures the size of a coin. Or consider the birds: roughly half of all migratory species travel at night, navigating by stars and magnetism, and city lights pull them off course into a maze of glass. Estimates of the annual American death toll from collisions run into the hundreds of millions. Hence the Lights Out campaigns, in which Chicago, Toronto, New York, and other cities ask buildings to dim during migration seasons—brief annual acknowledgments that the sky belongs to someone else.

Smaller casualties draw less notice. Moths, it now appears, are not so much attracted to lights as trapped by them—the glare scrambles the instincts they use to hold a steady course, and they spiral in until they die, which makes the porch light less a romantic cliché than a trap operating nightly. Studies find fewer caterpillars and pollinating insects around LED streetlights, in a world already worried about insect decline. Corals time their mass spawnings to the moon, releasing eggs and sperm in synchronies that artificial light measurably disrupts. Urban trees near streetlamps bud earlier in spring and hold their leaves later into autumn, their calendars scrambled by a permanent false dawn. Every one of these organisms evolved under a regime of strict alternation—bright, dark, bright, dark—and we have abolished the dark half of the contract in a single evolutionary instant.

We have done the same to ourselves, more gently. The pineal gland releases melatonin in darkness; the blue-heavy light of screens suppresses it, telling the body it is noon at midnight. Circadian disruption is implicated in metabolic disease, depression, immune dysfunction; the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies night shift work as probably carcinogenic. There is a bitter irony in the ledger: having conquered the night, we produced epidemic insomnia; having erased the boundary between day and dark, we lost the restfulness the boundary provided. Rest, it seems, requires a threshold. You cannot arrive at sleep if the day never ends.

How much has already gone? In 2016, an international team published the first complete atlas of artificial sky brightness, and its findings read like an obituary. More than eighty percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies. The Milky Way is hidden from more than a third of all people—from sixty percent of Europeans and nearly eighty percent of North Americans. For hundreds of millions of children, it is not a memory being lost but a possibility never known. We paved the wilderness, and then, finding the night inconvenient, we paved the sky above it too—the last landscape that had seemed too large to touch.

Yet darkness survives at the margins, and unlike most environmental losses, this one is reversible at the speed of a switch. Light pollution leaves no residue; turn off the lights and the stars return, immediately and completely. The International Dark-Sky Association, founded in 1988, now certifies parks and reserves where the night is protected by law: Natural Bridges National Monument in Utah, the first such park; the Aoraki Mackenzie reserve in New Zealand; the Atacama Desert of Chile, so dry and dark that the world's great telescopes cluster there like pilgrims. The engineering fixes are almost embarrassingly simple—shield fixtures so light falls down instead of up, dim them late at night, choose warm colors instead of blue-white glare—and they save money and energy while they're at it. Few environmental problems come with solutions this cheap.

From a lit room you cannot see the faintest stars; some things appear only against absence. This is true literally and otherwise. The night sky is the original instrument of scale—stand beneath it in a truly dark place and feel the vertigo of your own size, the recalibration that philosophers and astronauts alike have struggled to put into words. And the old segmented night, with its built-in hour of quiet wakefulness, hints at something else we traded away: enforced idleness, an unhurried interval in which the mind was allowed to drift without apology. Music needs rests; without them there is no rhythm, only noise. We have been deleting the rests.

Give your eyes half an hour; adaptation is slow and cannot be rushed, which is fitting. It is the oldest thing you will ever see, and it is still there, waiting behind the light switch.

We flattened it into a problem to be solved, and solved it, and are only now beginning to itemize what the solution cost. The remedy, mercifully, does not require returning to tallow and terror. It requires only a little restraint, a little shielding, a willingness to let one hemisphere of existence remain itself. Turn off the lights some night. Stand in the dark long enough for your eyes to remember their ancient work. The stars are not gone. They are only waiting, as they have always waited, for us to look up.

**The Vanishing Night**

On the evening of November 9, 1965, a faulty relay at a power station near Niagara Falls tripped, and the failure rippled outward through the grid like a stone dropped in still water. Within minutes, thirty million people across Ontario and the northeastern United States were without electricity. In New York City, elevators froze, subways stopped, and the skyline — for the first time in decades — went dark. And then something peculiar happened. People walked outside and looked up. Stories spread of callers phoning police stations and newspapers to ask about a vast, glowing cloud hanging over Manhattan. It was the Milky Way, which most of them had never seen from a city, and some had never seen at all. The details are probably embellished; such stories always are. But they survive because they capture something true: that most of us now live and die without ever meeting the night face to face. (~165)

We tend to think of night as simply the absence of day, a default setting, nothing in itself. But for nearly all of human history, night was a country with its own geography, its own laws, its own customs and dangers and liberties. Until roughly two centuries ago, every human being who ever lived spent half of every existence inside a darkness deeper than anything most of us will ever encounter — a darkness broken only by fire, by the moon, and by whatever courage a person could carry into it like a lantern. (~90) [shorter]

Consider the economics of light, because light was once a commodity like bread. A tallow candle — animal fat, rendered and wicked — smoked and stank and guttered, but it was what ordinary households could afford, and even it was rationed like sugar. Beeswax burned clean and bright and cost several times more, which is why it belonged to churches and the rich. The poorest families burned rushlights: dried rushes dipped in kitchen grease, giving off a feeble sputter worth pennies. To read by candlelight for an evening was to burn money. So people arranged their lives around the sun, not from piety but from arithmetic. They went to bed at dusk and rose with it, and the moon did the heavy lifting outdoors. Full-moon nights were working nights; the harvest moon, rising near sunset for several evenings around the equinox, was so valuable to farmers gathering crops that it earned its name. (~175)

And here is where the old night gets genuinely strange. The historian Roger Ekirch, combing diaries, letters, court records, and medical texts going back centuries, noticed something odd: again and again, writers referred matter-of-factly to "first sleep" and "second sleep," as though sleep came in two installments. They did. Before artificial light stretched the evening indefinitely, people went to bed a few hours after dusk, slept deeply for three or four hours, and then woke — not fitfully, but naturally, around midnight, into a calm interval that lasted an hour or more. Ekirch called it segmented sleep, and he found it described across centuries and across cultures. In the watch, people prayed, read by the light of embers, talked, made love — physicians of the era considered it the best time for conception — smoked, visited neighbors, or simply lay thinking while the house breathed around them. Then they returned to bed and slept till dawn. (~185)

This is not merely a curiosity of the archive. In the 1990s, the researcher Thomas Wehr ran an experiment that accidentally recreated the old world: volunteers given fourteen hours of darkness each day, mimicking a winter's natural photoperiod, gradually settled into exactly the pattern Ekirch had documented — a solid block of sleep, a quiet interlude of drowsy wakefulness, another block of sleep. During the interlude, their bodies seeped prolactin, a hormone associated with calm. The subjects described the state as something like meditation, a consciousness with no modern name. Which raises an uncomfortable thought: the millions who wake at three in the morning and lie awake, anxious, convinced they are broken — many of them may simply be experiencing an ancient rhythm that our brightly prolonged evenings have disguised, and that our panic about it turns into insomnia. We invented the eight-hour block, then pathologized everyone whose body remembers otherwise. (~175)

Night was also, for all its dangers, a kind of commons. The word curfew descends from couvre-feu — "cover the fire" — the bell that ordered hearths banked and citizens indoors, and behind the bell walked the watchmen with their lanterns and staffs. Cities feared the dark: footpads, cutthroats, ghosts, the devil himself, whom folklore stationed abroad between midnight and cockcrow. But the same darkness that threatened the respectable sheltered everyone else. The enslaved fled north along the Drinking Gourd, the dipper of stars that swings around the pole. Lovers slipped out. Poachers moved through the squire's woods. The poor, the outlawed, the restless — night was their territory, the one jurisdiction where the powerful were as blind as anyone else. Darkness confiscated wealth. For a few hours, the world reverted to something like equality, governed by whoever knew it best. (~165)

It was also a world heard more than seen. Deprived of sight, the preindustrial mind navigated by ear and nose: the creak of a signboard, a dog's bark changing direction, rain arriving over the hills, the smell of a neighbor's chimney smoke meaning someone was awake. And because the eye supplied so little, imagination supplied the rest. The dark was populated — by the mare, the demon of Old English nightmare, who sat on sleepers' chests and rode them through bad dreams; by revenants and will-o'-the-wisps; by every anxiety given a body. Folklore looks quaint now, but it functioned as technology: a set of rules and stories for managing fear in an environment where fear was reasonable. We replaced it with floodlights, which manage fear by abolishing the environment altogether. (~155)

Above all of this hung the stars. Under a sky unpolluted by artificial light, several thousand stars are visible on a clear moonless night, and the Milky Way is not a rumor but a fact of architecture — a river, a road, a tree, depending on the culture doing the naming. The Aboriginal astronomers of Australia read the dark lanes within it and saw the Emu in the Sky, a constellation made not of stars but of darkness itself, which tells you something about how closely they looked. Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific holding star paths in memory. Fugitives steered by the North Star. And every gaze upward was a gaze backward in time: the light of Andromeda, visible to the naked eye from dark places, left that galaxy two and a half million years ago, before any human being existed to see it. The night sky was the oldest library, open every clear night, free to anyone who looked up. (~195)

The conquest of this world began, as conquests do, with commerce. Whalers hunted sperm whales for the spermaceti in their heads, which burned brighter and cleaner than tallow, and by the eighteenth century the oceans were being emptied to light drawing rooms. Then came gas. In 1807, an entrepreneur named Frederick Winsor illuminated London's Pall Mall with coal gas to celebrate a royal birthday, and within a generation gasworks were humming on the edges of great cities, lamplighters were a profession with its own ladders and poles, and Paris — glowing — was earning the name City of Light. Travelers wrote of seeing the dome of brightness over a metropolis from miles away, a new kind of landmark: civilization announcing itself to the darkness, and beginning to push it back. (~165)

Then, in 1879, Thomas Edison's team produced a practical incandescent bulb, and in 1882 his Pearl Street station began sending electricity to a few dozen customers in lower Manhattan. The acceleration after that is familiar: arc lights, the white ways of Broadway, electric advertising shouting all night, factories discovering they could run around the clock, and finally the screen — a private sun we carry into bed. Within three generations, a rhythm that had governed every organism on Earth for four billion years became optional for one species. We did not merely illuminate the night. We redefined it: no longer a country with its own laws, but underused daytime, an inefficiency to be corrected. (~145)

The night, it turns out, was not empty. It was habitat. Consider the sea turtle, which has managed its affairs for a hundred million years using one simple rule: crawl toward the brighter horizon, which, on a natural beach, is the ocean reflecting the sky. A beachfront lined with hotels reverses the rule. Hatchlings pour from the sand and march inland, toward the glow, into roads and pools and exhaustion; entire coastal towns now pass lighting ordinances during nesting season, dimming themselves for creatures the size of a coin. Or consider the birds: roughly half of all migratory species travel at night, navigating by stars and magnetism, and city lights pull them off course into a maze of glass. Estimates of the annual American death toll from collisions run into the hundreds of millions. Hence the Lights Out campaigns, in which Chicago, Toronto, New York, and other cities ask buildings to dim during migration seasons — brief annual acknowledgments that the sky belongs to someone else. (~195)

Smaller casualties draw less attention. Moths, it now appears, are not "attracted" to lights so much as trapped by them — the glare scrambles the instincts they use to keep a steady course, and they spiral in until they die, which makes the porch light less a romantic cliché than a trap operating nightly. Studies find fewer caterpillars and pollinating insects around LED streetlights, in a world already worrying about insect decline. Corals time their mass spawnings to the moon, releasing eggs and sperm in synchronies that artificial light measurably disrupts. Urban trees near streetlamps bud earlier in spring and hold their leaves later into autumn, their calendars scrambled by a permanent false dawn. Every one of these organisms evolved under a regime of strict alternation — bright, dark, bright, dark — and we have abolished the dark half of the contract in a single evolutionary instant. (~180)

We have done the same to ourselves, more gently. The pineal gland releases melatonin in darkness; the blue-heavy light of screens suppresses it, telling the body it is noon at midnight. Circadian disruption is implicated in metabolic disease, depression, immune dysfunction; the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies shift work that involves circadian disruption as probably carcinogenic. There is a bitter irony in the ledger: having conquered the night, we produced epidemic insomnia; having abolished the boundary between day and dark, we lost the restfulness that the boundary provided. Rest, it seems, requires a threshold. You cannot arrive at sleep if the day never ends. (~135)

How much has already gone? In 2016, an international team published the first complete atlas of artificial sky brightness, and its findings read like an obituary. More than eighty percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies. The Milky Way is hidden from more than a third of all people — from sixty percent of Europeans and nearly eighty percent of North Americans. For hundreds of millions of children, it is not a memory being lost but a possibility never known. We paved the wilderness, and then, finding the night inconvenient, we paved the sky above it too — the last landscape that had seemed too large to touch. (~135)

Yet darkness survives at the margins, and unlike most environmental losses, this one is reversible at the speed of a switch. Light pollution leaves no residue; turn off the lights and the stars return, immediately, completely. The International Dark-Sky Association, founded in 1988, now certifies parks and reserves where the night is protected by law: Natural Bridges National Monument in Utah, the first such park; the Aoraki Mackenzie reserve in New Zealand; the Atacama Desert of Chile, so dry and dark that the world's great telescopes cluster there like pilgrims. The engineering fixes are almost embarrassingly simple — shield fixtures so light falls down instead of up, dim them late at night, choose warm colors instead of blue-white glare — and they save money and energy while they're at it. Few environmental problems come with solutions this cheap. (~165)

But it would be a mistake to defend the dark purely as wildlife policy, as though the stars mattered mainly to turtles and moths. Darkness is a precondition of certain kinds of seeing. From a lit room you cannot see the faintest stars; some things appear only against absence. This is true literally and otherwise. The night sky is the original instrument of scale — stand under it in a truly dark place and feel the vertigo of your own size, the recalibration that philosophers and astronauts alike have tried to put into words. And the old segmented night, with its built-in hour of quiet wakefulness, hints at something else we traded away: enforced idleness, an unhurried interval in which the mind was allowed to drift without apology. Music needs rests; without them there is no rhythm, only noise. We have been deleting the rests. (~175)

So consider an experiment. Find a moonless night and a map of dark places — they exist closer than you think, in state parks and high deserts and the pockets of rural darkness between towns. Give your eyes half an hour; adaptation is slow and cannot be rushed, which is fitting. Then look up and wait for the Milky Way to assemble itself out of haze, as it does, gradually, like a developing photograph. Somewhere in the process, remember that this view was the common inheritance of every human being who ever lived until very recently — that your ancestors fell asleep beneath it, woke in its middle hours, and told each other stories about it to keep the fear at bay. It is the oldest thing you will ever see, and it is still there, waiting behind the light switch. (~165)

The dark was never really the absence of anything. It was the other half of the world, with its own weather, its own peoples, its own laws of attention. We flattened it into a problem to be solved, and solved it, and are only now beginning to itemize what the solution cost. The remedy, mercifully, does not require returning to tallow and terror. It requires only a little restraint, a little shielding, a willingness to let one hemisphere of existence remain itself. Turn off the lights some night. Stand in the dark long enough for your eyes to remember their ancient work. The stars are not gone. They are only waiting, as they have always waited, for us to look up. (~135)

Ekirch called it segmented sleep, and he found it described across centuries and across cultures.
